title: Intro to Receptor Pharmacology
terms: "What the body does to the drug": absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination (ADME).
"What the drug does to the body": binding, activation, systemic response.
Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Elimination: the four pharmacokinetic processes.
How the drug gets into plasma (injection, transdermal, oral).
Injection routes listed under absorption on the S6 figure ("Intravenous, Subcutaneous, Intramuscular, etc.").
Where the drug goes in the body: bound in plasma, free in plasma, lipid, tissues A/B/C (S6 figure).
Distribution states on the slide: drug carried bound in plasma versus free in plasma.
How the body processes the drug, in liver (or other tissues).
Metabolism reactions listed on the slide (liver or other tissues).
How the drug exits the body ("out of the body"); S6 figure pictures kidney and intestine; the S5 diagram labels this step excretion.
OUTSIDE — confirm: time for plasma drug concentration to fall by 50%. Listed in objective terms, not defined on slides.
OUTSIDE — confirm: area under the plasma concentration–time curve; reflects total drug exposure. Listed, not defined on slides.
OUTSIDE — confirm: maximum (peak) plasma concentration after a dose. Listed, not defined on slides.
OUTSIDE — confirm: time after dosing at which Cmax is reached. Listed, not defined on slides.
OUTSIDE — confirm: lowest plasma concentration that produces the desired effect. Listed, not defined on slides.
OUTSIDE — confirm: meaning not given on slides; in anesthesia = minimum alveolar concentration. Confirm which meaning Dr. Basel intends.
OUTSIDE — confirm: lowest antimicrobial concentration that inhibits visible bacterial growth. Listed, not defined on slides.
OUTSIDE — confirm: concentration range between minimum effective and toxic levels. Listed, not defined on slides.
How the drug binds the receptor; described by KD.
What the drug does at the receptor.
What the drug does to the body.
Cell-free study of drug affinity for a receptor, ignores effect; [DR] plotted against [D]; described by KD.
Association rate constant: how fast the drug binds the receptor.
Dissociation rate constant: how fast the drug leaves the receptor.
KD = k-1/k1 (a ratio); drug concentration (M) at which 50% of receptors are bound.
How tightly a drug binds its receptor. Low KD = high affinity; high KD = low affinity.
Listed in S8 terms; not explained on slides. OUTSIDE — confirm: saturation equation with the same form as the binding curve.
In vitro study of how much signal a ligand causes; [drug] vs cellular effect; depends on binding + signaling; described by EC50.
Drug concentration (M) that elicits 50% of the maximal response in vitro.
Mass/volume or moles/volume; good for in vitro, where drug concentration at the receptor is measurable.
Mass/weight or mass/surface area; better for in vivo; brings pharmacokinetic principles into play.
In vivo study; drug dose vs % population with therapeutic effect; combines PD and PK; described by ED50.
Drug dose (μg/m2) at which 50% of the population shows a therapeutic effect.
Drug dose at which 99% of the population shows a therapeutic effect.
Drug dose at which 50% of the population shows a toxic effect.
Drug dose at which 50% of the population shows a lethal effect.
Drug dose at which 1% of the population shows a lethal effect.
LD50/ED50, a comparison of doses. Larger TI = bigger gap between therapeutic and toxic doses = generally safer drug.
Strength of the response a drug produces; S21 compares potency of the response (EC50) with binding affinity (KD).
No spare receptors: 1:1 receptors to pathways; response tracks % receptors bound; binding is the limiting step.
Spare receptors: more receptors than pathways; response exceeds % bound; signaling is the limiting step. S22: effect curve sits left of % bound curve.
Receptors beyond what is needed for full signal; create redundancy if receptors are deactivated.
Maximum response of the pathway; lowered by an irreversible inhibitor once receptor reserve is gone.
Permanently inactivates receptors; with spare receptors the curve shifts right at full effect until reserve is used up, then Emax falls (S23 figure).
Shifts the curve right (raises EC50) without lowering Emax.
Lowers Emax no matter the agonist dose; spare receptors can make it look competitive.
Adrenal tumor secreting catecholamines; surgical danger is hemodynamic instability from massive norepinephrine/epinephrine release.
Norepinephrine and epinephrine, released by the pheochromocytoma.
Receptor on smooth muscle mediating catecholamine response; spare α-adrenoceptors exist in many smooth muscle types.
Irreversible, non-competitive alpha-adrenergic antagonist given preoperatively for pheochromocytoma resection.
Risk when massive epinephrine overwhelms low-dose phenoxybenzamine because receptor reserve is not depleted.
traps: PK vs PD: pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME); pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body (binding, activation, systemic response). Don't flip them.
KD is a RATIO, not a difference: KD = k-1 / k1 (koff over kon). Off-rate on top.
Low KD = HIGH affinity; high KD = low affinity. Low KD means k-1 low and k1 high.
KD = binding (receptors bound) vs EC50 = response (50% of maximal response). Both in vitro, both units M.
Units trap: KD and EC50 are concentrations in M (in vitro); ED50 is a dose in μg/m2 (in vivo).
Concentration response = in vitro (binding + signaling); dose response = in vivo (binding + signaling + PK).
TI = LD50 / ED50 (lethal on top). Bigger TI = safer. Cisplatin 1.5:1 is the narrowest on the slide; amoxicillin/penicillin >>100:1 the widest.
EC50 = KD → no spare receptors, binding is limiting. EC50 < KD → spare receptors, signaling is limiting. Not EC50 > KD.
Competitive raises EC50 (shifts right); non-competitive lowers Emax. Spare receptors make a non-competitive antagonist look competitive.
Phenoxybenzamine is irreversible, non-competitive; it still looks like a right shift at low doses because spare α-receptors are not depleted. Raising the dose fails because its TI is too small.

quiz.stem: Which phrase from the lecture describes pharmacokinetics (PK)?
quiz.ok: What the body does to the drug
bad: What the drug does to the body
How the drug binds its receptor
What the drug does at the receptor
quiz.why: PK = what the body does to the drug (ADME); PD = what the drug does to the body.

quiz.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the pharmacokinetic ADME processes?
bad: Drug absorption
Drug distribution
Drug metabolism
quiz.why: ADME = absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination. Activation is a pharmacodynamic step.

quiz.stem: How is the dissociation constant (KD) defined from the rate constants k1 (kon) and k-1 (koff)?
bad: k1 divided by k-1
k-1 minus k1
k1 multiplied by k-1
quiz.why: KD = k-1/k1, a ratio with the off-rate on top.

quiz.stem: Drug A binds a receptor with a dissociation constant (KD) of 1 nM; Drug B binds the same receptor with a KD of 100 nM. Which statement is true?
quiz.ok: Drug A has the higher affinity for the receptor
bad: Drug B has the higher affinity for the receptor
Drug A has the faster off-rate from the receptor
Both drugs have equal affinity for the receptor
quiz.why: Low KD = high affinity; low KD means k-1 (off-rate) is low.

quiz.stem: Which definition matches the dissociation constant (KD)?
quiz.ok: Drug concentration at which 50% of receptors are bound
bad: Drug concentration eliciting 50% of maximal response in vitro
Drug dose at which 50% of the population responds therapeutically
Drug dose at which 50% of the population shows lethality
quiz.why: KD = concentration (M) at 50% receptor occupancy; the others are EC50, ED50, LD50.

quiz.stem: A researcher adds increasing amounts of drug to a constant amount of receptor in a cell-free system and plots [DR] against [D]. What does this study measure?
quiz.ok: Affinity of the drug for the receptor
bad: Magnitude of the drug's cellular response
Percent of population with an effect
Toxicity of the drug in the animal
quiz.why: A binding study measures affinity (KD) and does not care about effect.

quiz.stem: A researcher treats cultured cells with increasing drug concentrations and plots concentration against the cellular effect. Which study and parameter is this?
quiz.ok: Concentration response study described by EC50
bad: Binding study described by the KD value
Dose response study described by the ED50 value
Dose response study described by the TD50 value
quiz.why: In vitro, drug concentration vs cellular effect = concentration response study, described by EC50 (M).

quiz.stem: Which parameter is paired with the unit shown for it on the lecture slides?
quiz.ok: ED50 in micrograms per square meter
bad: EC50 in micrograms per square meter
KD in micrograms per square meter
LD1 in moles per liter of plasma
quiz.why: KD and EC50 are concentrations in M; ED50 is a dose in μg/m2.

quiz.stem: Why is dose, rather than concentration, the better measurement for in vivo studies?
quiz.ok: Drug concentration at the receptor in the body is impractical to measure
bad: Dose measurements remove all pharmacokinetic influences on the response
Dose measurements require knowing the local concentration at the receptor
Concentration can only be expressed as mass per unit of surface area
quiz.why: Dose does not need absolute or local concentration, but it brings PK principles into play.

quiz.stem: A dose response study in a population of dogs depends on which combination of effects?
bad: Binding and signaling effects, but not pharmacokinetics
Binding effects only, without signaling or pharmacokinetics
Pharmacokinetic effects only, without binding or signaling
quiz.why: Dose response studies combine PD and PK: binding, signaling, and PK effects.

quiz.stem: How is the therapeutic index (TI) defined on the slides?
bad: ED50 divided by LD50
TD50 divided by LD50
LD50 minus the ED50
quiz.why: TI = LD50/ED50, a comparison of doses; larger = safer.

quiz.stem: Based on the approximate therapeutic indexes on the slides, which drug has the narrowest margin between therapeutic and lethal doses?
bad: Digoxin
Cocaine
Morphine

quiz.stem: For an agonist, the EC50 is lower than its dissociation constant (KD). What does this suggest about the system?
quiz.ok: There are more receptors than signal pathways
bad: There is a 1:1 ratio of receptors to pathways
Receptor binding is the limiting step in signaling
Response magnitude equals the percent of receptors bound
quiz.why: EC50 < KD = spare receptors; signaling, not binding, is limiting.

quiz.stem: For an agonist, the EC50 equals its dissociation constant (KD). Which step is limiting in the signal pathway?
bad: The downstream signaling event
The drug absorption event
The drug metabolism event
quiz.why: EC50 = KD: response tracks receptors bound, so binding is the limiting step.

quiz.stem: A tissue has spare receptors. A low dose of an irreversible antagonist is added before the agonist curve is repeated. What happens to the agonist curve?
quiz.ok: It shifts right with no drop in maximal effect
bad: Maximal effect drops with no rightward shift
It shifts left with no drop in maximal effect
Maximal effect rises and the curve shifts left
quiz.why: With receptor reserve, full effect persists despite some irreversible inhibitor; non-competitive looks competitive.

quiz.stem: A dog with a pheochromocytoma receives low, tolerable doses of phenoxybenzamine before surgery, yet massive epinephrine release still causes a hypertensive crisis. Why?
quiz.ok: The spare alpha-adrenoceptor reserve is not depleted
bad: Phenoxybenzamine binds alpha-adrenoceptors reversibly
Epinephrine displaces phenoxybenzamine from receptors
Phenoxybenzamine is a competitive alpha antagonist
quiz.why: Spare α-adrenoceptors exist in smooth muscle; low-dose phenoxybenzamine (irreversible, non-competitive) does not fully deplete the reserve.

quiz.stem: In the same pheochromocytoma case, why is the phenoxybenzamine dose not simply raised until all alpha-adrenoceptors are blocked?
quiz.ok: Its therapeutic index is too small
bad: Its affinity for alpha receptors is too low
Its EC50 is lower than its KD value
Its effect is purely pharmacokinetic
quiz.why: Full blockade causes substantial toxicity that outweighs the benefit; the TI is too small.

quiz.stem: Which statements about spare receptors are correct? (select all that apply)
ok: They let a pathway signal fully despite some irreversible inhibitor
They can make a non-competitive antagonist look competitive
bad: They make the EC50 greater than the KD for an agonist
They make receptor binding the limiting step in signaling
They prevent an irreversible inhibitor from ever lowering Emax
quiz.why: Reserve keeps full signaling and masks non-competitive inhibition; once reserve is gone, Emax falls. Spare receptors give EC50 < KD and signaling is limiting.

flags: Slide citation typos

S25–S27 citation reads "Goodman & Gliman's The Pharmacologicalf Basis of Therapeutics" · correct title is Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics (OUTSIDE); typo only, no content impact.
Objective PK terms not defined
S4 lists half-life, area under the curve, Cmax, MEC, MAC, MIC, Tmax, therapeutic window but no slide defines them · definitions here are OUTSIDE — confirm with transcript.
MAC meaning unclear
S4 lists "MAC" with no expansion · anesthesia usage = minimum alveolar concentration (OUTSIDE); confirm which meaning Dr. Basel means.
Michaelis-Menten equation
S8 lists it as a term but no slide shows or explains it · OUTSIDE: same saturation form as the binding curve; confirm with transcript.
"LAST LECTURE" on S11
S11 tags concentration response studies as last lecture · 2026 prior lecture is LC29 Signaling Dynamics; confirm it matches (possible old-numbering carryover).
"KD is similar to EC50" (S10) vs EC50 < KD (S21)
S10 says KD is similar to EC50; S21–S22 show EC50 = KD only without spare receptors · use: similar format (concentration at 50%), equal only with no spare receptors.
Low KD = low k-1 AND high k1 (S10)
S10 says low KD means k-1 low and k1 high · OUTSIDE: KD is a ratio, so either change alone can lower it; use slide wording for the exam.
Excretion (S5) vs Elimination (S4, S6)
S5 diagram labels the last PK step excretion; S4/S6 use elimination (ADME) · use elimination for ADME.
Dose units
S14 says dose = mass/weight or mass/surface area; S15/S19 give ED50 in μg/m2 · use μg/m2 as on the slide; mg/kg dosing in practice is OUTSIDE.
Stop-and-think: does an antagonist have a KD? (S9)

Slide poses the question without answering · slide logic: both agonists and antagonists bind, so both have a KD; only agonists produce a response, so only agonists have an EC50 (OUTSIDE reasoning — confirm with transcript).
Figures checked against slide images

Checked against slide image: S17 values confirmed (ED50 ~5, LD50 ~10000, TI ~2000 μg/m2); S16 order ED50 < TD50 < LD50; S22 effect curve left of % bound curve with spare receptors, overlapping without; S23 curves: spare + irreversible antagonist = right shift, full Emax; no spare ++irreversible = Emax ~35%. Nothing left in doubt.
